strengths: Novel problem formulation: First systematic study of action-level backdoor attacks on TO models, identifying the critical gap that reward manipulation is ineffective for behavior cloning-based models
Thorough empirical investigation: Comprehensive analysis of key factors (target action selection, trigger design, reward manipulation) with well-designed ablation studies and multiple random seeds
Strong empirical results: 71.9% ASR with only 0.3% poisoning rate represents 105% improvement over Baffle and 27.2% over IMC, with excellent stealth (0.914 BTP)
Comprehensive evaluation: 972 experiments across 6 environments, 3 TO models, 3 target action types with careful ablations and robustness tests
Well-motivated technical approach: Each component (trajectory filtering, batch poisoning, alternating training) is clearly justified and shown necessary through ablations
Excellent reproducibility: Code available, detailed hyperparameters, clear algorithm specification, thorough experimental setup documentation
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Core components are straightforward applications—trajectory filtering (simple length-based), batch poisoning (poison 1 transition), alternating training (from existing IMC work). Novelty primarily in problem identification rather than technical innovation

Critical unsolved problem—trigger dimension selection: Paper shows dimensions critically affect success (Table 2: 0.91→0.0 ASR variance) but provides no principled selection method. Appendix F shows gradient-based approaches (Grad-CAM, NTK) don't correlate with effectiveness. Hardcoded to (1,2,3) limits generalization

Target action difficulty not characterized: Table 1 shows 0.11→1.0 ASR variance across action types; Table 17 shows 'arithmetic' targets are harder (0.536 CP vs 0.942 for '1'). No framework for predicting difficulty or understanding transferability

Incomplete baseline evaluation: Only Baffle and IMC compared; IMC from adversarial input literature, not designed for TO models. Anomalously low baseline CP values (e.g., 0.013) unexplained, raising fairness concerns
No defense analysis or mechanisms: Limitation A.3 briefly dismisses reward-based defenses but provides no systematic defense analysis or proposed countermeasures, limiting practical applicability

Lack of theoretical insight: Primarily empirical; no formal analysis of why/when TrojanTO succeeds. Why do certain state dimensions enable attacks? What TO model properties are exploited? No theoretical guarantees

Limited real-world applicability: All experiments in simulation (D4RL). Threat model assumes full training-time access (strong assumption). No analysis of deployment detection, trigger embedding stealth in practice, or real-world validation

Evaluation metric details: ASR success threshold ε not prominently specified; CP metric somewhat ad-hoc; 100 evaluation episodes may be insufficient for high-dimensional continuous control; normalization by clean policy could be problematic

strengths: Novel problem identification: First action-level backdoor attack against TO models, addressing an important gap between reward-based RL attacks and action-reconstruction-based TO models

Comprehensive empirical investigation: Systematic analysis of key factors (target actions, trigger dimensions, reward manipulation) with clear demonstrations that existing approaches are ineffective (Section 3)

Extensive experimental evaluation: 6 D4RL environments, 3 TO architectures, 3 target action types, rigorous ablations showing 105% improvement over Baffle and consistent robustness across diverse settings
Well-motivated methodology: Three components (trajectory filtering, batch poisoning, alternating training) are clearly justified with thorough ablations confirming individual contributions
Strong empirical results: 71.9% ASR with only 0.3% poisoning rate while maintaining 91.4% benign task performance demonstrates practical attack efficiency
Excellent reproducibility: Code promised, detailed hyperparameters documented, training resources specified, results averaged over multiple seeds
weaknesses: Unresolved trigger dimension selection: Despite identifying this as critical (Table 2), the paper provides no principled solution. Attempted Grad-CAM and NTK methods failed. Current approach fixes dimensions (1,2,3) without justification, limiting practical applicability

Limited algorithmic novelty: Components are straightforward applications of existing techniques (simple length-based trajectory filtering, standard batch poisoning, alternating training adapted from IMC [24]). Contribution is primarily in problem identification rather than methodological innovation

Missing defense mechanisms: Paper acknowledges reward-based defenses are ineffective but proposes no countermeasures, detection strategies, or defenses. For a security paper, this gap significantly limits practical impact and actionability

Design choices lack justification: Algorithm 1 switches to model-only updates after M/2 iterations without explanation. Trajectory length threshold is arbitrary. Harmonic mean (CP) assumes equal ASR/BTP weighting despite different real-world priorities

Incomplete failure mode analysis: Performance varies dramatically across settings (CP ranges 0.0-1.0 in Table 17). 'Arithmetic' targets much harder than '1' with limited explanation. High variance in some settings (e.g., Hopp fixed random: CP = 0.121±0.121)

Evaluation concerns: Some results show BTP > 1.0 (Table 4, GDT Walk: 1.089), suggesting backdoor improves performance—needs explanation. ASR threshold ε choice not discussed or justified with sensitivity analysis
Threat model limitations: Assumes post-training model modification access. Limited analysis of detectability through behavioral testing or how practitioners could identify poisoned models in practice
Sparse persistent backdoor evaluation: Section 5.3 uses only 3 environments. Context window limitation (K≤20) underexplored despite being important practical constraint

strengths: First systematic study of action-level backdoors against TO models, addressing an important and timely security gap
Valuable empirical insights on critical factors: target action selection and trigger design matter, while reward manipulation is ineffective
Highly practical post-training attack achieving 0.719 ASR with only 0.3% poisoning rate, significantly outperforming Baffle (0.369 ASR with 10%)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 D4RL environments, 3 TO model architectures, diverse target actions, with extensive ablations and multiple seeds
Well-maintained benign task performance (0.914 BTP) while achieving high attack success, demonstrating good stealth
Reproducible research with provided code and detailed hyperparameters in supplementary materials
Honest evaluation of existing defenses, revealing that standard methods fail for continuous action spaces
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (trajectory filtering, batch poisoning, MI-FGSM alternating training) are adapted from existing work; primary contribution is application to new model class rather than methodological innovation

Critical unsolved problem: trigger dimension selection is highly sensitive (Table 2: 0.915 vs 0.000 ASR), but gradient-based methods (Grad-CAM, NTK spectrum) fail to predict good dimensions; no principled selection method provided

Weak treatment of defenses: paper demonstrates vulnerabilities but only fine-tuning works (requiring retraining), and no novel defense mechanisms are proposed—ethically concerning for a security paper

Incomplete practical analysis: persistent backdoors limited to ~20 timesteps by context window; applicability to vision-based observations unaddressed; trigger injection mechanisms for real systems unclear
Target action selection problem unresolved: significant performance variation across action types (0.536 CP for 'arithmetic' vs 0.942 for '1'), but no method to predict or handle difficult targets
Evaluation metric concerns: ASR requires all action components within threshold ε, but ε not clearly specified; no sensitivity analysis for this critical parameter
Limited baseline comparison: Baffle is only directly comparable offline RL baseline; IMC from adversarial ML; missing comparisons with other recent RL backdoor methods

Hyperparameter sensitivity incompletely analyzed: multiple design choices (λ, MI-FGSM parameters, alternation frequency) lack strong justification; Table 19 shows performance varies significantly with alternation frequency
